lead.eyebrow: 📊 Markets Render Their Verdict — Oil Plunges as the World Prices a Post-War Energy Order
lead.headline: Stocks Surge, Crude Collapses: The First Trading Session Inside the Deal Sends a Definitive Signal
paragraphs: The global market verdict came swiftly and without ambiguity. As the G7 gathered for its summit in Evian, France on Monday — just hours after Washington and Tehran confirmed the framework deal — Brent crude fell roughly 4.7% to $83.78 and WTI slid about 4.8% to $80.90, while equities in Asia and Europe rocketed to record levels. Japan's Nikkei surged approximately 5%, South Korea's KOSPI posted similar gains, and the Euro Stoxx 600 climbed to a fresh all-time high as investors moved quickly to price out the inflation and growth fears that had dominated sentiment since the Strait of Hormuz closed in February. European natural gas tumbled more than 5% to €44.43/MWh; US natural gas eased 0.9% to $3.09/MMBtu.

Iran gave the deal deal substance on Monday, with a senior official telling Reuters the 14-point memorandum of understanding covers an oil sanctions waiver, nuclear limits, and the release of $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets — through a combination of direct cash transfers, regional cooperation mechanisms, and financial credit arrangements. The MOU also commits Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to all commercial vessels without tolls, while the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Trump, for his part, was characteristically direct: "Let the oil flow!" he declared over the weekend. A formal signing is confirmed for Friday, June 19, in Switzerland.

Yet the tape is not pricing a clean, zero-friction return of barrels. Mine clearing alone — the Strait is seeded with Iranian-laid mines — could take up to six months per US Congressional briefings, even though the US says it knows the location of every mine. Gulf fields shut in for months must restart; terminals and refineries damaged by strikes require repair. For Monday's session, that physical reality is less important than the direction: the war premium that carried Brent from the mid-$60s to a $144 war spike has now shed more than 40%. The energy-market story of 2026 is entering its final chapter.

news.headline: Nasdaq Surges, European Stocks Hit Record — First Session After Deal Paints a Clear Picture
news.body: The first full trading session after the US-Iran framework confirmation was a risk-on rout: Japan's Nikkei surged around 5%, South Korea's KOSPI posted similar gains, and the Euro Stoxx 600 climbed to a fresh all-time high. US futures pointed sharply higher at the open. Oil and gas — the two instruments that soared with the war — gave back the most: Brent fell about 4.7% to $83.78, WTI slid nearly 5% to $80.90, European TTF natural gas tumbled over 5% to €44.43/MWh, and US Henry Hub slipped 0.9% to $3.09/MMBtu. The message from markets was unambiguous: war risk is being priced out, and fast.

news.headline: Iran Confirms 14-Point MOU: Oil Sanctions Waiver, $25B Assets, Nuclear Limits
news.body: A senior Iranian official confirmed Monday that the memorandum of understanding with the US covers three core areas: an oil sanctions waiver allowing Tehran to resume crude exports and receive related revenues; the release of $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets through direct cash transfers and financial credit arrangements; and limits on Iran's nuclear enrichment activities. The MOU calls for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz without tolls and the lifting of the US naval blockade, with follow-on technical talks over the 60-day ceasefire extension to address the nuclear file in full detail.

news.headline: G7 Summit Opens in Evian — Leaders to Address Hormuz Demining and Lebanon
news.body: The G7 summit opened Monday in Evian, France (running June 15–17), just hours after the US and Iran confirmed their framework deal. Hormuz demining is a top agenda item: G7 members the UK and France have expressed interest in assisting with the mine-clearing operation once the conflict formally ends. Trump and other leaders are also expected to address support for Lebanon, whose ceasefire with Hezbollah is tied to the broader deal, and to discuss the path to a permanent nuclear accord with Iran. The summit runs through Wednesday — a day before the signing ceremony in Switzerland.

news.headline: Europe Signals EU Sanctions Relief; Japan, UK, Germany Welcome the Deal
news.body: European leaders from the UK, France, Germany, and Italy welcomed the US-Iran framework and signaled they were prepared to lift EU sanctions on Tehran in exchange for verifiable steps to curb Iran's nuclear program. Japan welcomed the deal and the prospective Hormuz reopening, which would ease supply chains across Asia. World leaders called for swift implementation and a durable framework. The broad chorus of support from G7 partners adds diplomatic momentum heading into Friday's signing — reducing the probability of a last-minute breakdown.

news.headline: The Long Tail: Mines, Idled Fields, Damaged Terminals — Barrels Won't Flow Overnight
news.body: Even a clean Friday signing faces months of physical work before supply normalizes. US Congressional briefings say full mine-clearing of Hormuz could take up to six months, though the US Navy says it knows the location of every Iranian-laid mine and could clear them faster under a cooperative agreement. Beyond the strait, Gulf producers must restart fields shut in since February; refineries, terminals, and pipelines damaged by drone and missile strikes require inspection and repair. The physical implementation timeline — not the diplomatic one — now governs when barrels actually move.

news.headline: US Crude Stocks Drew 8M Barrels Week Ending May 29 — EIA Next Report June 18
news.body: US commercial crude inventories fell 8.0 million barrels in the week ending May 29, dropping to 433.7 million barrels — roughly 3% below the five-year average. The following week (ending June 5) saw an additional 7.2 million barrel draw. The string of consecutive large draws signals physical markets remain tight even as the geopolitical premium deflates. The next EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, covering the week ending June 12, lands on Wednesday June 18 — the first inventory print fully inside the post-deal tape.

events.name: G7 Evian Summit — Demining Framework & Lebanon Support
events.impact: Any concrete G7 commitment on Hormuz demining — which navies, which timelines, what safe-passage protocols — directly accelerates the supply return and pulls crude lower. Conversely, public friction among G7 members over sanctions relief terms, or Iranian pushback on nuclear limits at the summit margins, would reinject premium and support prices.
events.market_impact: Directional: ±$3–5/bbl on demining and framework announcements.

events.name: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (Week Ending Jun 12)
events.impact: The first inventory print fully inside the post-deal market. After consecutive large draws, the signal shifts from supply-side tightness to how fast demand is responding to cheaper crude. Another draw plus firm refinery runs would buffer the glide lower; a surprise build would accelerate it.

events.name: Official Signing Ceremony — Switzerland
events.impact: The signing converts an MOU into a binding treaty. A clean ceremony with the Hormuz reopening timeline confirmed is the bearish base case — Brent could test the high $70s. Any delay, no-show, or dispute over nuclear enrichment limits or the $25B asset release would be the single largest upside catalyst left on the calendar.
events.market_impact: Largest scheduled catalyst this week. Binary, headline-driven.

events.name: Hormuz Mine-Clearing & Gulf Field Restarts
events.impact: The bridge between a signed deal and barrels in the water. US says mine locations are known; cooperative removal could be fast. But damaged infrastructure and shut-in fields add a separate lag. Any visible evidence of mines being removed or tankers transiting Hormuz would pull crude lower; evidence of delays keeps the floor.
events.market_impact: Structural — governs the pace and shape of the supply return.

events.name: Nuclear Talks & Sanctions Relief — Permanent Peace Framework
events.impact: The MOU defers the hardest questions — enrichment levels, highly enriched uranium stockpiles, and full sanctions relief — to follow-on talks during the 60-day ceasefire extension. Constructive progress erodes residual premium; a breakdown before the window closes would reintroduce tail risk and could violently reprice the curve higher.
events.market_impact: Defines whether the low-$80s holds or retests $90+.

paragraphs: The market has spoken, and it speaks clearly: the war premium is gone. From the $144 April spike to $83.78 today, Brent has shed more than 40%. Equities from Tokyo to Frankfurt are making new highs. The Strait of Hormuz deal is moving from rumour to text to ceremony. This is no longer an event risk — it is a logistics trade.

My read on today: Monday's session was a referendum on the deal's credibility and the verdict came in decisively — buy everything except energy. That verdict is rational. The oil sanctions waiver, the $25 billion in frozen assets, and the nuclear-limits commitment are more substance than we've seen from any prior round of talks. The G7 is formally behind it. Europe is ready to remove EU sanctions. The chorus is loud and the direction is clear. But the market is pricing the deal; it has not yet priced the restart.

The bigger picture: The gap between a signed piece of paper and barrels flowing through Hormuz is still measured in months, not days. Mine clearing, field restarts, terminal repairs — these are engineering problems, not diplomatic ones. That gap keeps a floor under crude and means the glide to the high $70s or below will be slow and conditional. The risk profile is genuinely two-sided: the bearish base case is a clean Friday signing and visible demining; the bullish tail is a last-minute dispute over enrichment limits or asset-release mechanics.

My call: Brent holds $79–$88 today, biased lower into the Friday signing but with meaningful upside if the nuclear or asset terms hit a snag. I remain neutral-to-bearish on direction and still prefer owning optionality. The war premium is gone. The implementation premium is all that stands between here and the high $70s — and that is a timeline question, not a diplomatic one.
